title: Where the conveyor loop begins
prompt:
Implement findEntry(head): head starts a conveyor of linked nodes that may loop back on itself; return the node where the loop begins, or null if there is no loop.

- In Python the function is find_entry(head) and returns None for no loop.
- Each node is an object with val (an integer) and next (the next node or null; None in Python). In Python, nodes are dicts: node["val"], node["next"].
- The list has 0 to 10,000 nodes. Values can repeat, so compare nodes by identity (=== in JS, is in Python), never by value.
- Use O(1) extra space: no sets or maps of visited nodes, and do not modify the nodes.
- The provided cycleEntry / cycle_entry driver builds the list from values (linking the last node to index tailTo, or no link when tailTo is -1) and returns the index of the node you return (-1 for null). Tests call the driver.
hints: A slow pointer (1 step) and a fast pointer (2 steps) meet if and only if there is a loop.
Let the loop start a steps from head. Where they meet, the slow pointer is exactly a steps (mod the loop length) short of returning to the loop start.
After they meet, move one pointer back to head and advance both one step at a time. They meet again exactly at the loop's entry.

solution.explanation: Fast gains one node per step on slow, so inside a loop it must land on slow; with no loop it reaches the end. At the meeting point the distance forward to the entry equals the head-to-entry distance modulo the loop length, so single-step pointers from head and from the meeting point arrive at the entry together.

complexity.notes: Floyd's algorithm: if the entry is a nodes from head and the loop has c nodes, the meeting point is a steps (mod c) before the entry.

followUps: Return the length of the loop as well.
Use the same idea to find the duplicate in an array of n + 1 values in the range 1..n.
